utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- every morning to be taken by surprise. Yes. Mr. Registrar, could you again call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning, Mr. Corn. I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony is still binding. And, Mr. Russo, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let's go to page 27 of your expert report, and this is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This is a part of your answer to question 1 of the addendum. I'm looking at the middle of the second-to-last page -- I'm sorry, second-to-last paragraph on that page, where you state: "The record indicates that prior to launching Operation Storm, General Gotovina had not ordered the use of indirect fires against military objectives in Knin, even though those objectives were well within range of his indirect fire assets. This is a significant factor in my assessment of his decision-making process, for it corroborates the inference that the employment of this asset during Operation Storm was nested within his overall operational concept. Because of this, it is unlikely that General Gotovina would have wasted this valuable resource on an objective with little or no tactical value. It also seems difficult to ignore the fact that this record also reinforces an inference that General Gotovina never acted with the intent to use this asset for the purpose of harassing or deliberately targeting the civilian population of Knin, as there was no fire on Knin prior to Operation Storm." Professor, you obviously place significant weight on the fact that General Gotovina never shelled the alleged military objectives in Knin prior to Operation Storm, but I'd like to put to you that this fact actually adds nothing to the analysis of whether his use of artillery during Operation Storm was lawful. And let me see if I can try to demonstrate that. First, if General Gotovina had fired artillery at the alleged military objectives in Knin prior to Operation Storm, would it still be your opinion that it was lawful?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had been fired at military objectives and the effects did not cause or weren't anticipated to cause an excessive degree of collateral damage in relation to the objective, then that would have been a lawful use of artillery, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me be a little more specific. Well, first, when you made the statement that I read, were you referring to the fact that General Gotovina had never shelled the same military objectives that you opined about in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement that you read is based on, again, the facts and assumptions provided, that the general's organic fire support capability had Knin within range prior to launching Operation Storm. In my view and what I was attempting to express there, the fact that those assets were not employed prior to launching the main tactical effort --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Corn, if you would not mind if I stop you. That was not the question. The question that was put to you was not further to explain the portion read to you, but was whether you understood the facts available to you to include that General Gotovina had never shelled the same military objectives that you opined about in your expert report before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- the facts that I understood upon which that paragraph is based is that from the point in time where those objectives were within range of his assets, he did not shell the same military objectives prior to Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, maybe you can help me out with what I'm missing here. Prior shelling on the same objectives in Knin wouldn't have changed your analysis in any way, because on the one hand you say if he didn't shell military targets in Knin in the past it corroborates a lawful use during Operation Storm; and on the other hand you say, well, if he had shelled those targets in the past, it would have been lawful anyway, so I don't see how that could lead to any inference other than the one you've already drawn.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was exactly what I was attempting to explain. The -- let's just call it the -- I don't want to use the word "restraint." The decision not to use the asset prior to the commencement of the main tactical effort was relevant in my mind for two purposes. First off, if he had used the asset previously against nonmilitary objectives or in an indiscriminate manner, then consistent with what I stated yesterday I think that is evidence you would have to consider in the totality of the record when assessing the propriety of his use during the operation. But I also think it was relevant - and this is what the word "nested" and "wasted" was attempted to convey - it's relevant because it indicates or supports the inference that his actual employment of artillery was designed to support his priority of effort. And I guess I should have maybe explained the word "nested," but the concept is that it's connected, it's within the overall objective. Now -- now, a use prior to that against a lawful military objective wouldn't necessarily undermine the inference that it was a nested use, but the pattern of employment, the connection to the jump-off point or the beginning commencement of the ground tactical operation, in my view is a significant element in my analysis of what his intended purpose for that use was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, did you consider as an alternate explanation the discussion during the Brioni meeting as a reason why the shelling might not have happened prior to Operation Storm itself?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And specifically I'm talking about President Tudjman's comments about using a counter-attack from Knin as a pretext for using artillery and his comments about the political situation being so favourable at the time of Operation Storm. Couldn't that also be a reasonable interpretation for why General Gotovina did not shell in Knin prior to Operation Storm, but instead chose to do it during the military operation?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it could be an explanation. I was asked to render my honest opinion. That's what I did. And in my honest opinion, the pattern of employment was consistent with an operationally sound decision-making process, and that's -- I don't think that that paragraph indicates it's conclusive. It's the only inference you can draw from the pattern of employment, but what I was trying to emphasise was from an operational and tactical perspective there's logic in linking your priority fire support mission with the priority ground tactical assault. So the answer is: Yes, I think that's a possible explanation. In my opinion, it's not the most logical explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Looking at page 29 of your report, subsection (f), one of the assumptions you point out is that the HV observed a civilian evacuation "subsequent" to Martic's evacuation at 1645. Do you see the part I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, first of all, does it matter or did it matter to your analysis of the use of artillery whether civilians evacuated at all?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that prior to that I noted that one of the assumptions or facts that I was provided indicated that General Gotovina believed or assumed or had information indicating that even prior to initiation of the operation, there had been a substantial exodus of civilians from the city. I think that is absolutely a relevant consideration for a commander using artillery in a populated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you explain why you believe that's a relevant consideration?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, as I think any reasonable commander would know, that the higher the density of the civilian population, the more exposed the civilian population might be; the timing of the attack; and the relationship between that timing and the civilian population are all factors that you must consider when conducting that balance between your anticipated effect and the anticipated collateral damage or incidental injury. And I think at another point in the report I emphasized that all of these elements are relevant in a target decision-making process when the anticipated means of warfare is indirect fire in a population centre, a civilian population centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I understand the significance of the concentration of civilians generally, but what I want to focus on is the assumed fact about a civilian evacuation subsequent to Martic's evacuation order. What I'd like to know is: Would it matter to your analysis if in fact the civilian evacuation that the HV purports to have observed here occurred significantly prior to Martic's evacuation order?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would it matter? Well, what would matter to my analysis was what information General Gotovina was aware of. If in fact there were no civilians in the city when he launched his operation but he anticipated there was a substantial civilian population, then in my opinion that is the fact, his knowledge or his expectation or - to be more precise - as the law requires his anticipation is what would influence my analysis. What I was attempting to do, as I said before, is to provide an opinion based on the information that I was told was information that he understood to exist at the time. So -- and if he knew that there had been an even greater evacuation of the town prior to commencing the operation, it wouldn't change my analysis related to his obligation to distinguish between lawful objects of attack and civilian objects, but it would influence my critique of his assessment of the balance between objective and collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, let me ask you to assume then that General Gotovina becomes aware that after he begins shelling in Knin but prior to Martic's order there begins a significant civilian evacuation of the town, would that change your analysis in any way?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are -- I mean, there are so many variables embedded within that question. Just one example. If he had preplanned an indirect fire strike on an area, for example, to deny it as a potential muster point or a crossroads or a bridge and he becomes aware that that area or crossroads or bridge is packed with civilian evacuees, then that would have - should have - a profound impact on his analysis conducted prior to that time. In the alternative, if, for example, he had considered striking a target where there was a senior military commander living in an apartment building with 300 civilians and he learns that all the civilians have evacuated, then a target that he may have excluded previously would once again become legally viable. So I think it would depend on where the civilians were, what the target set was he was considering, what effect he sought to achieve, and how the evacuation would influence his assessment of the proportionality analysis. But once again, I want to emphasise, it would not free him to simply sail, Well, there are no civilians in the city, now I can attack everything, I can bombard everything. Because while civilian personnel might be out of the city, there is still substantial civilian property, and he must consider that in his equation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let's move to page 30. At subsection (d) you assume that General Gotovina refrained from employment of indirect fires to harass the civilian evacuation or deliberately target civilians in the evacuation observed on the afternoon of the first day of the operation. Now, this, I believe, is the one assumption which I believe you pointed out earlier as the one you recalled from the meeting and specifically asked for permission to include in your analysis; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, first, just to clarify. What do you mean when you say "refrain from harassing the civilian evacuation." Can you explain what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assumption that I contacted Defence counsel in relation to this portion of the report was that at some point during this evacuation process General Gotovina became aware that there were enemy military personnel or enemy personnel, obviously, if they're not military they're not enemy, there were enemy personnel co-mingled with this flow of individuals exiting the conflict area or the battle space, whatever term you want to use. I thought at that point it was significant that he didn't even, to my knowledge, seriously contemplate whether he could treat that as a lawful military objective because of the co-mingled nature of the population. Now, if he had assessed that as a military objective, it would obviously have raised a significant question of whether it would have been a proportional attack. Probably is about as difficult a dilemma in that regard as you could hypothesise. A retreating enemy is not per se defeated, but he's not at that moment combat-effective. Co-mingled with a substantial number of civilians, inevitable severe casualties to civilians if you use indirect fire. My assumption was the very nature of that co-mingled target led him to make the judgement that we're not going to engage it. Now, I don't know if, even assuming that judgement was made, it was driven primarily by his humanitarian instinct or by an operational assessment that: I want other members of the enemy force to know that if they choose to drop their weapons and run they will have an escape route. That may have been his primary motivation, but the fact remains that I thought it was significant that he never seemed to contemplate placing that exodus under attack to kill or harass the co-mingled military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, did you consider as an alternate explanation whether General Gotovina, if he intended to actually encourage civilians to leave, that that might be a reason why he wouldn't shell the columns?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, it's similar to the previous question, linking back to the Brioni transcript. If you look at the commentary to Article 51 and its discussion of the prohibition on indiscriminate attack, the relationship between that prohibition and distinction, and very specifically the prohibition on attacks intended to spread terror among the civilian population, the commentary notes that terror in the area of war, terror among the civilian population in the area of war is oftentimes an inevitable consequence of combat. And that the prohibition is focused on whether or not the commander acted with a purpose to inflict that terror, to cause that terror. If General Gotovina, in my view, in the Brioni meeting was essentially saying to the president, There is a natural consequence that is ongoing. I don't need to make any civilian the object of attack. Even if he, in my view - and I said this yesterday - even if he thought as an operational matter the exodus of the civilian population as consistent with the -- to the commentary to Article 51's view as a natural response to what they see going on around them, the effects of war, even if he thought that that might affect the determination of his enemy to stand and fight, I don't think that it's improper for him to consider that effect. What's improper is if he used his combat capability to produce that effect as a purpose. So yes, I did consider that, but as you know from our dialogue yesterday, I don't -- I don't believe that the Brioni transcript in the broader context establishes as the only possible or reasonable inference that he embraced the proposition that he would deliberately employ combat power for the purpose of spreading terror among the civilian population in order to achieve either a strategic political effect or a military effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to understand what happens at this moment. I'm listening to questions and answers. You give explanations how you understand the situation, and you are mainly focusing on a commander who's pursuing legitimate strategical aims. Mr. Russo says, But if that commander would have something totally different on his mind, that is, to expel the civilian population, then you start explaining that if he would not have that on his mind but if it would be an effect that it would not be under all circumstances acceptable. And then you start explaining why you do not share Mr. Russo's assumed belief or whatever you call it, that this was on General Gotovina's mind. So finally it comes down to you disagreeing on what was on his mind, perhaps we could shorten this discussion because I think you would agree - that's at least how I understand your answer - that if General Gotovina, as it was put to you by Mr. Russo, had on his mind to use military means, apart from re-gaining the territory, also to drive out the civilian population, and them not to return, that that would be illegitimate. And then you're back to where we are at almost all the questions, that is, that you're focusing on possible explanations of events, meetings, whatever. So it could well fit into a fully legitimate operational context. Mr. Russo focusing on other matters. So I see two gentlemen with different approach, who not necessarily disagree with each other on the issues what is legitimate, what is not legitimate. Of course you have said you have to be very careful. Certain weapon systems are not, per se, illegitimate, but it depends on the circumstances. And then whatever Mr. Russo puts to you -- you say, Well, it ain't necessarily so, isn't it? I'm just trying to follow this, and it's repeating itself quite often. Could we perhaps -- is there any way that we could shorten the discussions to say if your assumption is right, then I would agree. But I'm not convinced on the basis of what I've seen that that's a right assumption. And then I think we know where we are because this -- I'm just trying to analyse what I see happening during this cross-examination. Mr. Russo and Professor Corn, I'm addressing both of you because you're two partners -- not in crime, but at least in this -- in the interaction which I see and hear before me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would like to emphasise on that kind of more global perspective, having read the Brioni transcript, and throughout this whole report, I always had in the back of my mind there might be an alternate illicit motive to some of this. So I considered it in relation to all of these answers, and I tried to explain in the answers why, in my view, the totality of the record supported an alternate rational inference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what you are doing is if Mr. Russo puts to you what apparently his view or approach on the matter is, you say that matters are rather complex and that this could be the case, that could be the case, this could explain, that could explain. And Mr. Russo in response to your explanations puts to you that could it not be that and that and that. And that's what happens already for quite a couple of hours. I'm not saying that it's -- certainly enlightens your positions, but there seems to be disagreement on what would be reasonable to assume rather than that there is disagreement on what would be legitimate or not legitimate, given certain assumptions. Could you please keep this in the back of your mind for the continuation of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, if I could just respond briefly. Part of what I'm doing -- I didn't hear the Court to consider this. I'm sure the witness understands, but let me just see if I can clarify. Part of what I'm doing is attempting to demonstrate to the Trial Chamber and point out to the witness the fact that the assumptions and facts which he bases his opinion on and from which he draws inferences favourable to General Gotovina, that those same facts and assumptions, the ones I'm pointing out as a matter of fact, are not inconsistent with the Prosecution's theory of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's perfectly clear that that's what you're seeking to establish. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, you were not provided with any information regarding the rate of fire, of artillery fire, on Knin throughout the course of the day on the 4th of August. You were told to assume a surge during the morning. If at times during the day on the 4th of August the rate of fire was as low as four to five rounds per hour falling somewhere in the town, can you explain in your opinion what military advantage General Gotovina could expect to achieve from that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was maybe somewhat ironic that as I was contemplating writing this report, I happened to be in Buenos Aires and visited the Malvinas memorial and was reminded of a conflict that I had done some significant study on earlier in my military career, the Falklands which is referenced in the report as a historical analogy. I think, as I stated in the report, that the purpose of that sporadic fire was harassment and interdiction. It was connected to the general's operational objective of demonstrating his full-spectrum control over the fight, preserving the initiative, denying the enemy initiative. These are effects that are identified at the very beginning of Colonel Konings report, and these are the classic purposes of artillery. What I thought was so interesting - and I placed this in the report for this reason, and again this is my opinion - is that was the analogy between the priority of effort at the tactical point of attack but the need to disrupt enemy C3I logistics and manoeuvre in the rear area between Storm and the battle -- the final phase of the Falklands battle and the ammunition supply realities. Most people don't know that when General Menendez capitulated, the British howitzers were down to approximately two rounds per two. One of the assumptions that I based this opinion on, or two of the assumptions, the first was that the priority of effort was the tactical fight for fire support, organic fire support; the second was that the general had a limited supply of ammunition for his fire support assets. And so the pattern of employment once again, in my view, is consistent with a priority of effort to support the close fight. You surge your artillery at the time of day or at the point in time where your need to blind the enemy and fix the enemy is at its highest. And as I -- and you and I -- and the other assumption was that he didn't have unlimited resources and, therefore, at other points in the battle, other times of the battle, he has to use sporadic fire to keep the enemy fixed, disoriented, essentially off balance. And I think that could explain reasonably that employment pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, in regard to the number of civilians in Knin, we've already talked a little bit about that. But I want to be clear about the assumptions upon which you based your report. Page 28 in your report, the top of the page, subsection (a), the assumption you relied on is: "Although Knin may have had a population of up to 15.000, there were indications that the number of non-mobilised civilians remaining in Knin on the eve of Operation Storm was as low as 3.000." Now, Professor, I'd like your clarification on this because it -- at least it occurred to me that the use of qualifying words and phrases like "may have had indications as low as" seem to suggest no real degree of certainty. So I'd like your assumption. Did you assume there were about 3.000, or somewhere between 3 and 15.000?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't assume factually that the actual numbers -- it's -- the lead-in to that is that General Gotovina, in making this judgement, it is probable that General Gotovina considered the following facts related to the situation. What I assumed was that if the general had a report that the population had been reduced to about 3.000, he probably wouldn't have said or thought, That is absolutely accurate. A commander in his position I believe has learned through experience that ground truth is rarely exactly consistent with reports. I mean, this goes back to the discussion yesterday on the order to relocate the headquarters. But he reasonably, based on this report, in my view, could have considered that the population, the civilian population, had in fact been substantially reduced, and we had the discussion about the curfew already and the specific time it ended, but that as a result of the conflict and the timing of the curfew, that there might be a residual benefit from that in terms of the location of that population when he initiates his operation. So it was what I believed would have influenced his decision-making that I considered, not whether or not that was factually true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, given the importance that you rightly place on the concentration of civilians in and around the objectives to be attacked, did you seek any specific information from the Gotovina Defence about, first of all, the efforts that General Gotovina made to determine what the concentration of civilians actually was?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I asked the Defence to provide was the information that they believed was supported by the record related to what the general would have known at the time. And obviously -- well, maybe not obviously. I withdraw that. And because I am being asked to render an opinion that is going to turn significantly on applicability of the proportionality rule, one of the facts or assumptions that I expect to be given information about is the population as he -- evidence of the population that was available to him. I did -- the answer to you is: No, I did not ask them what he had done to verify that because that was the assumption I was given, that he was made aware of this information. And he -- my understanding of the anticipation of how the law works is that a commander - I've said this before - a commander relies on the members of the staff responsible for providing information on targets, on the civilian population. In fact, this is referenced in the -- again, in the commentary to AP I, to Article 51, rarely will a commander have the opportunity to personally verify all the facts and assumptions provided by the staff. So what was important to me was what the Defence, as best the Defence could offer me, what the record had established in terms of information that would affect his decision-making process at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we shorten this discussion a bit. I fully understand your testimony. You say these and these reasons, a reasonable commander would have considered. Now, I put it very bluntly in the other direction to say, Well, I know that there were 15.000, there's still 3.000 left, so therefore I have to use artillery to drive them out. I mean, would this information be consistent with such an approach if, of course just for argument's sake, that was what the commander had on his mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if that was his intent, then certainly, that could be a use of artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The same for the curfew hours, to say if we want to drive them out, let's use artillery just at the time they get up and know they have to leave, we stop after that so they can leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course it's very cynical what I'm doing, but I'm trying to find out --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what keeps us busy for such a long time on fitting facts, assumed facts, in one theory or another.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that could be an illicit calculus of course. As I stated in the report, Your Honour, I think that there would be other optimum times to use artillery, but, yes, if he anticipated that he was trying to demonstrate -- or if his intent was to demonstrate: The minute you get up, you're going to be fired at, then you could say that that would be rationally consistent with that illicit purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, we are again in the situation I described before. Not to say that it's totally useless, but I think we could do that more quickly. Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, I'd now like to discuss your analysis and opinions relating to the alleged military objectives identified for you by the Gotovina Defence. And I'd like to begin with the shelling of Milan Martic. Now, looking at page 23 of your report, that's the beginning of your answer to question 1 in the addendum. The last sentence of the first paragraph you specifically mention relying on General Gotovina's operative assumption that: "Pressuring or, if possible, eliminating Milan Martic could drastically influence the decision-making process of the RSK and ARSK leadership and potentially force capitulation quickly and with less military and civilian casualties." Now, I want to parse this out because it seems to me to contain two distinct military advantages, that is: Number one, pressuring Milan Martic; number two, eliminating him. First, would you agree that if General Gotovina engaged in the artillery attack against Milan Martic, only with the objective of killing him or injuring him, would you agree that that would not be a proportional use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I have enough expertise on the effect -- the capability of a 130-millimetre barrage on that building and the nature of the building to answer that conclusively. I think it would depend on the assessment General Gotovina was given by his fire support experts as to the relative probability or improbability of achieving that effect. And the importance of that effect in his view as it related to the operational situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Moving to the other military advantage of possibly pressuring him, I'd like your assistance in understanding your position on this. Do I have to understand that you believe General Gotovina was justified in deciding that an artillery attack aimed at Milan Martic would produce the military advantage of potentially forcing a capitulation? Is that ... ?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that that's an ipso facto conclusion. What I think -- well, let's start. If General Gotovina thought that killing or disrupting this individual's ability to participate in command and control and the decision-making process of his enemy, if he thought it had no significance whatsoever, then that's a low-value target. And the fact that it's in a civilian building I think would render it off limits, because if you don't think you're going to get value out of it -- I mean, you can't say just because it's somebody connected to the military it's automatically of tremendous value. My assumption is that he believed that this individual was an important component in the enemy's decision cycle. And this goes back to the first day. Understanding the notions of initiative, tempo, dictating the terms of the battle. If he believed that this individual was an important component in that decision-making process of the enemy, then disrupting this individual's ability to perform that function might and probably would contribute to the uncertainty, the confusion, and hopefully the paralysis of the enemy's command and control structure. That disrupts the enemy, denies them initiative, and protects the initiative that he's attempting to establish in order to set and dictate the terms of the fight. So that's what I meant by "pressure." In my view, if you destroy communications and this individual is in a building some distance from the command and control centre and is unwilling or unable to physically make himself present, it has an effect on his subordinates even if he's not killed, even if they suspect he might have been killed, that produces an effect; and that effect, the value of that effect, is directly linked to the anticipated role this individual plays in that enemy decision-making cycle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, at section 4 of your addendum, that's at page 10, you state: "The advantage gained by targeting a place or thing must be 'definite.' Again, the purpose of this qualifier was to prevent unfounded speculation or conjecture on the value of targeting a place or thing would produce. However, no commander can know with absolute certainty what the value to be gained -- the value to be gained from attacking a target. What the 'definite' qualifier is intended to prevent is general speculation on some attenuated value of target engagement. So long as the commander acts with a good-faith basis that the target engagement will produce a tangible, operational, or tactical advantage for his force, the qualifier is satisfied." Now, Professor, under your own interpretation General Gotovina had to have a good-faith basis that an artillery attack on Milan Martic would produce a tangible advantage; not that it could, that it would. And if there's an admittedly potential advantage in influencing him, what I'm having trouble understanding is how you can say that firing artillery at Milan Martic could push the RSK towards capitulation, but, you would agree with me, it could also push them towards retaliation. And it's that possibility that he can't know and it's that possibility that runs afoul of his requirement to use that weapon only when he will anticipate a direct and tangible military advantage?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with your interpretation of the law and what it requires. The discussion of the -- in the commentary that explains that definite military advantage is designed to eliminate rendering or justifying an attack based on speculation or conjecture relates to the equation of: If I can produce this effect, do I have a good-faith basis to believe that it will contribute, make a substantial or actual contribution to my effort? I think it is almost inevitable that when a commander decides on attacking a place or a thing or even enemy forces, there's always the possibility that it will have an effect that was not anticipated. For example, if you're attacking an enemy and you destroy a bridge in order to prevent the enemy from receiving reinforcements, you may, in fact, produce an outcome where the defending enemy that's isolated becomes more determined to defend himself because he has no escape route. And that's always a risk in warfare. In my view, what Article 51 requires is a good-faith assessment of the connection between the anticipated effect and the operational effort that you're connecting it to. To me, speculation would be something more like this in this context: You know based on your intelligence that although this person is the titular head of the armed forces, he plays no significant role whatsoever in the planning, execution, adjustment of the enemy's operations, but you say, But who knows, maybe if I confuse him or I kill him, one of the enemy commanders might be disturbed by that and that might confuse the situation for a while and I achieve an effect. To me, that's speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you again. I understand your answer to be the rule is about avoiding pure speculation as to the military effect. There is a range between pure speculation and hundred per cent certainty, somewhere in between, not on the speculation side, but also the rule does not require the certainty, certainly not. And then Mr. Russo introduces, as far as the military effect is concerned, a rather difficult element. That is, if the military effect depends on other people making decision on the basis of that - so I'm not talking about destruction of a bridge, I'm not talking about killing an enemy, I'm not talking about hitting a tank so that it can't move anymore - but if you -- the military effect depends on human decision-making in response to that, then we have -- I think for examples we have another day or two or three to see how that could work out under all kind of circumstances. It could be that they immediately capitulate. It could be that they would seek the support of ten other nations to fight against the Croats. That's on this scale. Mr. Russo, it's clear that we are dealing with this scale and that humane -- human decision-making may make it very difficult to assess where exactly we are on that scale because it needs further assumptions. Human decision-making is usually a bit unpredictable, although some experience we may have that can give us some guidance in what to expect, and that makes the military effect moving a bit from pure speculation to the certainty. That's clear. We're on the abstract level. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with that as well, Mr. Russo?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sure, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think I -- yes, yes, I -- well, then it seems that you agree on these matters. Let's move to the next subject. Mr. Russo, I can imagine that, of course, was Mr. Martic at home? Could the attack been televised so as to influence decision-making in the field? Would -- I mean, I could give you a list of 20, 30, if not 40 assumptions which could have an impact, big impact, small impact on how to look at this matter. But we know what the witness knew because he has written this down. We have still a bit of a grey area the discussions he had for the Defence team, which we have no detailed information about. So we could go on with this for another hour or two hours easily. But whether that would assist the Chamber is - should I say - speculative or uncertain, or where would it be on the range whether it would assist or not assist the Chamber? Rather low. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm afraid the Court's being a bit cynical about my examination. It was not my intention to put to the witness all number of scenarios regarding the possibility. I simply wanted his explanation of where the admitted uncertainty in the effect, how that factored into his analysis. We now have his answer, so I'll move on. I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, I don't think I answered that portion of the question. I mean, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- I've tried to establish now a couple of times that the disagreement may lie in an area where finally the witness couldn't help us out because that is the solidity of the assumptions, further details of assumptions, facts. So therefore, I'm not saying it's useless to establish that there are -- could be different opinions if we would know everything about certain matters, but that can be established more quickly, I would say. And I'm also addressing you, Professor Corn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To see where the real disagreement lies, where the expertise of the witness brings us into a direction which is substantially different from the Prosecution's position, and where it seems that the primary focus may be in fitting events into what a reasonable commander would have done opposite to what apparently your focus is, Mr. Russo, how the events fit in if the commander had a different agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor Corn, let me give you an opportunity to address my last comment to Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just want to make it clear that, obviously, I believe the anticipated effects are part of the equation. That's why I say the commander has to decide whether or not -- if he can achieve the effect he seeks to achieve, will it offer a definite military advantage? And weaponeering is part of that process, the selection of the means to achieve the effect. So I do believe that he has to consider whether the capability he proposes, or that has been proposed for use against the target, could achieve the effect he desires to achieve. If he's told, This cannot achieve the effect you want to achieve, then he's got no -- he knows there's no anticipated military advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, you're aware from reviewing Brigadier Rajcic's testimony that during the course of combat activities the HV fired the 130-millimetre cannons at other places where, according to their intelligence, they believed Martic to be present. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I recall that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And let me just give you a few specifics from Rajcic's testimony. He gave as one example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, could you guide us to the relevant pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President. This discussion is at transcript page 16394 and goes on to 398.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rajcic gave as one example of this one particular place where this happened, a building known as the old hospital in the down-town area. He testified that it was a sudden target which emerged during the course of combat and which had not been planned. He testified that this happened during the highest intensity of the combat, that he was provided by an intelligence official the X, Y, and Z coordinates of a location with the word "Martic" next to it. And he was told that it was a building, and on that basis he proceeded to fire. Now, Professor, I'd like your opinion about the propriety of essentially targeting any area where Martic happens to run into during the artillery attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President. I think in the spirit of completeness, I do believe that the Prosecution has charged this facility as a police facility in their indictment of Martic. I think that was part of our discussions concerning the stipulation on Martic, that this old hospital facility in the Martic indictment was alleged to be a police facility and that we had some discussion about that. If I am incorrect, counsel, please let me know, but I think that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. President, I object to informing the witness of what Mr. Kehoe believes the stipulation to have been. It also doesn't -- let me finish. It also doesn't, first of all, have anything to do with the question I asked. I'm also not sure, because I don't have the stipulation in front of me, whether that applies to the time-period, the 4th of August, that we're discussing. But in any case, it doesn't really apply to the question that I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in the full spectrum of information to be given in a hypothetical, I would think that the Prosecution wants to give the full explanation of what this building is based on their prior statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, what the Prosecution wants to do is for the Prosecution to decide. If you consider that they have given incomplete information, of course you can add this to the information and see whether that changes the opinion of the expert. I think it would have been a matter appropriately be dealt with in re-examination. Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, would you like me to re-ask the question?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First off, once again, Your Honour, I would like to emphasise that my -- I was asked to render an opinion on the propriety or reasonableness of General Gotovina's decision-making process, not Marko Rajcic's. If you give me a hypothetical where a military commander or officer, responsible -- staff officer responsible for ordering an attack knows that an individual has gone into a hospital, an active hospital, I don't care if it's the president of the country or the commanding general of the enemy armed forces, that does not render the hospital a lawful military objective. So if that officer or decision-maker says, Well, look, we've been ordered to kill or injure X person, Martic, and he's in a hospital now so that means we can attack the hospital, I think that's illicit. But I think it does relate back to the expectation that a superior commander has legitimately -- that subordinates will execute orders consistently with the law. Now, there are other variables, and I'm sure the Tribunal knows this. If the enemy is misusing the hospital as a military objective, then the law requires a warning to the enemy to cease and desist unless the situation is so immediate that a warning would jeopardise the friendly forces. I don't see that as the hypothetical presented. But if General Gotovina identified the enemy Commander-in-Chief as a high-value target and tasked his subordinate elements to act on that designation, he should reasonably anticipate that they're not going to attack a hospital in order to achieve that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, it's my fault. I didn't mean to suggest that this was an active hospital that Martic ran into. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have on the basis of the word "hospital," "stara bolnica," we've now spent quite a while in court. Of course, Mr. Russo, you said a building known by the name "old hospital." This created the whole of the confusion. What apparently Mr. Russo wants to ask you is how -- what your opinion is about legitimacy of when you receive information, Mr. Martic is here, Mr. Martic is there, Mr. Martic is there, to just attack all those positions. That's what you intended to -- yes. Now, Mr. Russo, when Mr. Kehoe made his objection, you could have intervened and you could have taken away the problem by just rephrasing your question; that would have saved us quite a bit of time. Please proceed. And perhaps you could answer that question, because I understood your question, Mr. Russo?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the situation is obvious, the hypothetical obviously presents a very difficult situation. You're talking about actionable intelligence that -- that one of the highest-value targets on the commander's priority target list has been located in an extremely time-sensitive situation. I believe what the law requires of the subordinate commander executing the mission is to do his level best, acting in good faith, based on the information that's available to assess the risk of collateral damage or incidental injury. I think if I were in that situation I would presume that whatever building he went into, unless I was told he's in a military building, I would presume that the attack would be inevitable, there would be -- it would be inevitable that there could be civilian collateral damage or incidental injury. I -- if you don't have actual knowledge but you know it's a populated area and you know he's not a military building, I think you almost have to presume that. And therefore, to me the question will be: What type of building did he go into? How much do we know about the building? And how does that influence our judgement based on our known value of achieving the effect? And then the next element is: How much damage are we going to have to inflict to attempt to achieve the effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'd like your help in explaining -- I understand that this is clearly a difficult hypothetical, it's a difficult situation, but if the subordinate commanders you indicate - and granted this is happening during the course of combat - if the subordinate commander doesn't possess the information, you indicate that he needs to assume -- or at least you would assume that there would be civilian collateral injury. But if he doesn't know, for example, how many people are in the building, how can he actually conduct the proportionality analysis? Because he doesn't know how much incidental or collateral damage it may cause.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the law requires him to make a good-faith judgement based on the information available. The better your information, the more -- the better your judgement's going to be. I mean, we know this. This hypothetical is analogous to the efforts the United States made to kill Saddam Hussein during Operation Iraqi Freedom. He moved around from area to area; the commander had his best estimates of the civilian population; the US commander, obviously, was able to rely on exceptionally capable collection means. If he had ignored his opportunity to gather that information, he would have been derelict. I think -- my point is that the commander has to make a judgement in the heat of battle based on the best evidence he has, and he also has to consider, once again, timing, location, what is the pattern of civilian behaviour that he knows about as the Court indicated on the first day? If this commander is aware that the pattern of behaviour is the minute the curfew ends everybody is out in the street, that is a significant element in the critique of his judgement process. But if you're asking me do I think that a commander must have absolute certainty or close to it on the ground situation before authorising an attack, I think the answer to that is no. He has to act on his best effort to obtain information and the best information he's able to obtain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll be moving on to a new area. It's probably a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that Mr. Waespi took the role Mr. Misetic has on the Gotovina team, that is, to see that we wait until the translation has finished. At the same time, I would rather avoid the need of such a traffic policeman on either side. So if we could slow down that would certainly assist the interpreters, and it might even improve the quality, to the extent possible, of transcript and translation. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just have an oral motion. I could do it outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I could do it just before we come back. I can do it whenever Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom and for you to proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Trust me, Mr. President, this will be very brief. Mr. President, I address myself to the adjudicated facts in the Martic case by the Trial Chamber of the Martic case and addressing myself again to paragraphs 20 -- excuse me, 285 to 294, and we ask the Court under Rule 94 (B) to take judicial notice of the fact that the Trial Chamber in Martic ruled that the old hospital in Knin was, in fact, a police -- RSK police facility and that would be our motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like the proper amount of time to respond to the motion. I don't need 14 days. I just need to go have a look at that. I don't think it's going to be a problem, but I don't want to do it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would the break be enough? Because I take it that Mr. Kehoe considers a decision relevant for the examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- Mr. Kehoe, your reference to paragraphs 285 to 294, is that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's the Trial Chamber's decision, Mr. President -- excuse me, Trial Chamber's judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Trial Chamber's judgement, and did they adopt adjudicated facts or want you -- or are you seeking this Chamber to adopt --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from the trial judgement the facts, adopting them as adjudicated facts, in the Martic trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as taking judicial notice, I would ask this Chamber to adopt the adjudicated facts by the Martic Trial Chamber pursuant to Rule 94 (B).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was a bit unclear --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether the Martic Chamber adopted them as adjudicated facts or whether you wanted this Chamber to adopt them as adjudicated facts, that is, adjudicated by the Martic Chamber. We'll have a look at it, and we'll -- before we decide, we'll hear from Mr. Russo. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, have you verified the Martic transcript or the Martic judgement?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've had a look at the paragraphs indicated by Mr. Kehoe. We do not agree with the fact that he proposes, that being transcript page 32, lines 22 to 24, the fact that the Trial Chamber in Martic ruled that the old hospital in Knin was, in fact, a police -- RSK police facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Since I was in a meeting during the break, I'll now on the spot verify what we're talking about. Is there any way that you try to stipulate -- is it the formulation, or is it the substance?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It's a bit of both, Mr. President. If we changed it to -- it was an RSK detention facility between 1991 and 1992, we have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I take it, Mr. Kehoe, that you wanted us to take judicial notice of a fact contained in the Martic trial judgement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- now let me just ... Then we have to find in the Martic judgement. Mr. Corn, this will take us a few seconds to get to the right document and to see. Loading takes a few seconds. Mr. Kehoe, I have in front of me an electronic version of the judgement, 12th of June, 2007, and you wanted us to take judicial notice from paragraphs 285 to 294, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then have a look. And what ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's on Sanction, if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I've got it in front of me at this moment. What fact exactly would you like us to take judicial notice of and what paragraph can we find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is -- the paragraphs would be the totality of the 285 to 294, and the position we would like to take judicial notice of is that this facility, this detention facility that was contained in the old hospital was, in fact, a detention facility run by the Ministry of Justice. If I can turn in addition to these paragraphs to paragraph 414 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, if -- I would first like to find exactly -- I'm now at 285. Where is for the first time a section of - let me just have a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The first sentence in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- paragraph 285 designates the old hospital in the centre of Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And there it says: "From the summer of 1991, the Ministry of Justice of the SAO Krajina took over control ..." and then in "... 1992, the Assembly of the RSK formally established the District Prison in Knin." Now, apparently there's some concern with Mr. Russo that this was not forever. Mr. Russo, could we see, is there any way to find out that it was limited to a certain period in time or --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, the paragraphs pointed out by Mr. Kehoe, read them, they only indicate the 1991 to the 1992 time-frame. In respect of the evidence in our case as to what the use of that building was, I'll refer the Trial Chamber to the evidence of Witness 56, whose testimony through 92 ter Exhibit P289 under seal, indicates what the -- this particular facility was used for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in the context of adopting adjudicated facts, the Chamber is not in a position to start comparing what evidence there is in this case. Mr. Kehoe, the objection is that the Martic judgement is insufficiently precise, unspecific, as to whether that function of the old hospital still did exist in 1995. What is your response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My response to that, Judge, is the following, and I would like to include to the summary paragraph 414 that I omitted before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My response to that, Judge, is number one, Your Honours can take those facts and weigh them accordingly. We are simply at this point asking the Court to take judicial notice of those facts in the Martic judgement. He we would be more than willing to argue how this plays into what a reasonable commander might have expected or would have or could have expected this facility to be used for at the operative time-frame. Putting aside that it wasn't. We all agree that it wasn't a hospital. So at this point we're not looking for a stipulation, we're not asking for a stipulation from the Prosecution; we're just asking the Chamber to take judicial notice of these adjudicated facts, and we will argue the weight to be accorded them and what the significance of those facts are when we move to final argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the Prosecution has presented its case. Adjudicated facts are serving a party to be relieved from its duty to present evidence on a certain matter. Now, apparently this is a fact which would -- disfavourable to the Prosecution's position, whereas the Prosecution has already presented its evidence. So I am trying to understand how this procedurally fits into what the adoption of taking judicial notice of adjudicated facts is created for. And I'm now reading 414.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, at this moment and on the basis of your submissions, the Chamber cannot take judicial notice of a fact which would include that the old hospital was functioning as a detention facility in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- at this point, and I not only ask the Court to take judicial notice of that time-frame, I just ask that the Court take judicial notice of the factual findings in the Martic judgement, and then we will make our arguments from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you know how we are dealing with adjudicated facts. You clearly describe what fact you want to be judicial notice taken of, and then to say exactly where to find that in the judgement. And apart from -- but I take it that that would not create a major problem, but of course we would have to check whether there was any challenge to this fact on appeal. I do not know. I have not checked whether we find anything about it in the appeals judgement. I would not expect it to be, but we have to be precise in taking judicial notice of facts established by other Trial Chambers. And as I said before, the Trial Chamber is not at this moment in a position to take judicial notice of the functioning of the "stara bolnica" in 1995 as a detention facility, whereas it appears from that judgement that at an earlier point in time it did function as a detention facility. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me just clear something up. First of all, we agree, at least the evidence has been presented by Witness 56, that in fact in 1995 the facility was being used as a detention facility. Mr. Kehoe's suggested fact was that it was an RSK police facility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So if that's the only detention facility, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see light in the tunnel. I see light in the tunnel. He we could not take judicial notice of something a witness said before this Chamber, but of course you could make a stipulation. Mr. Kehoe earlier said he would not seek a stipulation, but it seems that there is an opening. The stipulation would be that the "stara bolnica" in 1995, and may I take it in August 1995 -- any further specification as far as the dates are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't think we need any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is during Operation Storm -- at the beginning of Operation Storm served as a detention facility for the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: For the RSK civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the RSK --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It actually is for the Ministry of Justice, but that's an issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may -- if I could -- I'm being pointed to something on the record, if I might have one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Corn -- well, being a lawyer, you are either thrilled by it or bored by it. I'll leave that open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm moving around the courtroom here, Mr. President, but there was further evidence by Witness 56 under seal on page 3606 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can't deal with evidence under seal. What about, Mr. Russo, is it at this very moment that relevant? Because we earlier established that you were mainly aiming at Mr. Martic being around, and then the word "hospital" was used. That triggered Mr. Kehoe to get on his feet and to say that the hospital was, in reality, a detention facility. Then you're not happy with his intervention. Then Mr. Kehoe pursued the matter by asking us to take judicial notice of. It's clear that we can't take judicial notice of. I now ask myself: How relevant is it for the remaining part of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not going to be continuing on with questions about that particular facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I have no objection if Mr. Kehoe wants to give an assumed fact based on detention facility or anything that he wants to formulate his assumption on. I'm not going to be objecting to an assumed fact he provides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And then during the next break if you really feel that there's any relevance in it, you'll certainly sit together and find out exactly what to stipulate upon. Let's move to the questions you would like to ask to Mr. Corn. Mr. Kehoe, may I take it that the motion to take judicial notice of, that that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, it's withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The oral motion is withdrawn. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, moving now to question 3 in your addendum, which appears at page 31, and this is where you discuss the reasonableness of General Gotovina's decision to order artillery fire on some of the alleged military objectives in Knin. And I'd like to begin with the ARSK HQ, and you state: "While it would be unlikely MBRLs would achieve a 'destructive' effect, their use against this target is understandable. The area effects of this weapon ... could have been relied on to degrade C3I by destroying communications antennas, cables, and equipment." Professor, first, you were not provided with any information or assumptions about communications antennas, cables, or equipment being exposed outside the ARSK HQ, so that's an assumption that you added on in addition to what you were provided with; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And given your acknowledgement that MBRLs are area weapon systems and Brigadier Rajcic's testimony about the concern of using those in a civilian neighbourhood, why is it that you say they could be relied on to strike a point target like a cable?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my initial report I was asked directly the question as to whether use of a multiple-launch rocket capability would be essentially per se improper in a populated area. I'm responding essentially to a broad opinion in Colonel Konings' report. I noted then that in the abstract the use of a multiple rocket capability in a populated area would seem to raise concern because it is fundamentally an area-denial or destruction or disruption asset. And Colonel Konings notes this in his discussion of different types of artillery assets. But I went on to note, in a manner I believe is consistent with the commentary to Article 51, that virtually no weapon system is per se unlawful under the prohibition against indiscriminate attack, and that in the vast majority of situations it's much more significant how the means is employed, what effect it seems to achieve, than it is to focus on the system itself. And that's a paraphrase from the ICRC commentary to Article 51, which goes on to say the concern about weapons that are per se indiscriminate during the drafting of the treaty focused on means of warfare such as the use of fire, flooding, and even nuclear weapons, that type of extreme. So I had to ask myself in responding, essentially, to Colonel Konings' initial conclusion: How could use of an area system like a multiple-launch rocket be reasonably justified in this scenario? Now, I -- you asked me just before this, did I assume that connected to a headquarters are vulnerabilities of communications capability, antennas, wires, communications rigs. I did assume that. I think any reasonable intelligence officer would make an analogous assumption. Now, you're absolutely correct, I wasn't provided a fact or assumption that said the intelligence officer for the general knew that as a fact or didn't know that as a fact. So I am treating this the way I believe a reasonable officer, reasonable commander, would have treated the target. With the limitations on ammunition re-supply, the priority of effort to support the close battle and the effect, desired effect, of disruption of C3I, I believe it would have been reasonable to assess a potential vulnerability to that C3I capability that could be exploited by the use of a multiple-launch rocket. That rocket can destroy antenna equipment. It can destroy cables. It can destroy vehicles that support that equipment. It can destroy un -- less-than-hardened facilities that support that C2 function. It has other effects as well. If you are effective in achieving those destructions, then the enemy is going to have to try and restore that capability. You have demonstrated to enemy personnel your ability to affect the area of the headquarters. That might reduce or degrade the effectiveness of any restoration effort. And you can even go one step further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Professor Corn, you've given some reasons why you could use it. I'm certain that you could give us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- another 20 or 30 or 40. I don't know, Mr. Russo, whether you're interested to hear all of those.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's why I believe it could be a reasonable use, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, my question was actually a bit more focused than that. Given what you know about Rajcic's testimony, that not even the 130-millimetre cannons could be directed only at the ARSK HQ building and that the MBRLs --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I would ask for a specific reference in the transcript where Mr. Rajcic said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I understood a moment to be a short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I believe I almost have it here. Just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you already on a day so that we could ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm actually checking my earlier examination because I did, in fact, have the citation. Mr. President, if we turn to -- my apologies. One second. If we look at transcript page 16284, lines 11 through 15. "Q. And with respect to those two targets, the Main Staff of the RSK, and the communications centre, were the 130-millimetre guns and 122-millimetre rocket systems, were they capable of being fired at those targets and only hitting those targets and nothing else around them? "A. No."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now back to my question, Professor. If Brigadier Rajcic says if you fire 130-millimetre cannon, 122-millimetre rockets at the building, they're not only going to hit the building, they are going to hit things around them, how then can you say the rockets can be relied on to hit a cable which may be coming out of that building?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you don't fire the rocket to -- for the rocket to -- the tip of the rocket to hit the cable. I would refer you back to Colonel Konings' report and his discussion on rockets and their effects. Rockets normally contain sub-munitions. That's why it's referred to as an area-denial or attack capability. You fire the rocket to an area, the salvo, on the expectation that the effect of the rockets will damage or destroy those aspects of the enemy's capability that are vulnerable to that blast effect. And this is -- this is in the doctrinal recitation from Colonel Konings' report. On page 11 he notes: "They," rockets, "tend to provide a high rate of fire, yet find difficulty in supplying and loading their munitions to match potential consumption" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Professor Corn, sorry to interrupt you again. The question was whether you could say that rockets can be relied on to hit a cable. The answer clearly was that you would not hit that individual cable, but I do understand your answer to be that if you fire rockets, that the damage may be such that if in the area there are cables and where you would expect to be cables that they would suffer damage and, therefore, would have this effect. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And I apologise. The only point I was trying to emphasise was that my assessment is based on the same doctrinal understanding of the effects and use of rockets that is embedded in Colonel Konings' report, because I think that's useful, as well as his discussion of the neutralisation and harassment effect of the fire support system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, even assuming that the weaponry used against the HQ could destroy communications equipment, that would only have an effect on the communications capabilities of the command -- so if those same communications capabilities could be knocked out by destroying or disabling another facility without endangering civilians and posing no greater risk to General Gotovina's forces, wouldn't you agree that he was obligated to choose that alternative rather than firing artillery at the HQ in order to accomplish the same objective?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree based on a qualification. The effect that the commander seeks to achieve is disabling the C3I capability for a defined period of time. The commander could assess, for example, a vulnerable relay station or an antenna in another location, but the assessment has to include communications redundancy. It has to include restoration potential. And so, as again is referenced in Colonel Konings' report, the fire sport element is used in a synchronised manner to best achieve the effect. If you -- if I assume, which I think is the assumption of your question, that the commander ultimately concludes that I can achieve the identical effect by targeting an asset that is not in a populated area, then I believe the commander bears an obligation to select that course of action. But the effect has to be identical, not just the immediate consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, I don't want to get into a very long discussion about this, but your emphasis on the word "identical," Article 57 only requires obtaining a similar military advantage, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are you disagreeing with that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. If I use the word "identical" to -- if that's too restrictive -- I understand what Article 57 says, it's in my report. Similar, but -- the point is it's the effect on -- the effect he seeks to achieve. And by the way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep matters short.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you used the word "identical." Mr. Russo draws your attention to the word "similar" contained in Article 57. And you say my quotation might not have been in every respect accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, the only other justification you offer in this section for firing on the ARSK HQ is: "Enemy forces required to move in and around the area would be under significant apprehension that they would be made the object of future area-denial attacks, potentially degrading their ability to accomplish their mission." Now, based on this language are you saying that shelling the area around the HQ in order to cause possible apprehension among soldiers is a legitimate use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the right set of circumstances, the answer is yes. As a matter of fact, again, the doctrinal recitation discusses suppression and refers to an objective not to inflict substantial loss on the enemy, but to reduce its own vulnerability, forcing the enemy to reduce its own vulnerability, for example, by moving or delaying operations to another time. Suppression is designed to influence the enemy's decision cycle and course of action. In the same report it refers to one of the doctrinal effects of artillery as shock effect. Therefore, to be used sparingly to achieve maximum shock effect at specific phases of the battle. This is the doctrine that's embedded in Colonel Konings' report. So disrupting the enemy's ability to manage the battle by inflicting the psychological fear on the enemy personnel associated with being placed under artillery attack is a doctrinal mission of rocket artillery.
