And in addition, as I said earlier, if you are effective in blowing up or damaging those cables and wires and antennas, in order to restore command, control, and communications, somebody has to go out and repair that equipment, some military member. You will degrade, just as the doctrine says, the enemy may be forced to delay that process in response to your use of artillery that does not have an intended destructive effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, do you honestly believe that using four to five rounds per hour is going to make enemy soldiers apprehensive about walking into and out of this building?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- I am grateful to say I have never been under artillery attack. I have been in an operation where I have been in the proximity of indirect fire use and impact. And, yes, I do believe that if you begin your operation with a surged salvo against military objectives, then your periodic use of attacking those objectives will serve to increase the apprehension by your enemy as to whether you can dictate at any moment the terms of the battle. And this is why I drew the analogy to the attack in the Falklands, because I thought it was quite a similar dilemma the commander faced with a similar course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, if UN personnel could find their way into and out of this building during the course of the day and if civilians in fact ran into the building in order to seek shelter, how can the possibility of making soldiers apprehensive about doing the same thing really justify a risk of causing collateral damage and incidental injury to civilians?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the commander is making a decision based on an anticipated effect within the operational constraints he confronts. There -- when he makes this decision, I'm sure if he had the ability to destroy the building in a manner that was consistent with IHL, he would have preferred that course of action. But in my assessment of the reasonableness of placing this objective under attack or these objectives in the manner reflected in the facts and assumptions, I had to consider whether it was unreasonable to attempt to achieve that continuing effect in the manner in which he did, not whether I thought I was certain he would in fact achieve that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Regarding the shelling of the ARSK HQ on the 5th of August, the following day, and your assumptions about what was still in the town at that time, you testified - and this is at draft transcript page 31, lines 14 to 17, that's from yesterday's transcript - "My assumption, and that's what it was, Mr. Russo, was that at 5.00 the next morning the operational commander makes a judgement that there is still a C3I capability, even if it's a residual C3I capability in those buildings that housed those enemy headquarters."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just to correct the reading, counsel, I think it's C3I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there was no confusion about that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, you made that assumption, as you indicate, based on another assumption which was provided to you by the Gotovina Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assumption -- the fact provided by the Defence was that the attack -- the main effort resumed the following morning, that there had been an order that General Gotovina was aware of from the RSK headquarters to displace the command/control function from Knin to a rear location.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes. And from that assumption which was provided to you, you made the further assumption that General Gotovina made a judgement that there was still a residual C3I capability in Knin. And my question to you is: Did you call the Gotovina Defence to ask them whether that further assumption you made was supported by the evidence; and if so, why didn't you mention that earlier?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. And the reason I did not was because of the pattern of operational employment and the broader facts and circumstances they had provided, and the -- the underlying assumption that the purpose of the use of artillery on the second morning was analogous to the purpose on the first. If that assumption is flawed or the facts don't support it, then the opinion changes dramatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let's move now to the northern barracks, which you address on page 32, and that's at subsection (b). Here you state that this facility has the same C3I value as the ARSK HQ and that in addition: "Targeting this objective would also offer the added value of potentially fixing enemy reinforcements or, at a minimum, disrupting their ability to muster and manoeuvre." And later in the paragraph you repeat the same advantage regarding targeting cables and equipment, as you indicated for the ARSK HQ -- I'm sorry, later in the paragraph you repeat the same advantage regarding the apprehension of soldiers moving to and from the target. Now, reading this I -- I read those as essentially the same military advantage, fixing potential enemy reinforcements and disrupting their ability to move around is the same as causing apprehension in soldiers to move to and from the target. Is that the same thing or is there a distinction there that I'm missing?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- well, in -- when I wrote that, I was basing it on the non-exclusive list of potential military objectives within Knin that indicated the ARSK Main Staff was the primary C2 and command, control, and communications facility; in contrast, the information I was provided indicated that at the 7th Krajina Corps headquarters at the northern barracks, there were also elements of a brigade and other support units. In the context of the effect on the headquarters personnel, yes, if you are less inclined to go out and fix an antenna, re-run a land-line, or even come and go to your place of duty, that's the effect that I think artillery could be anticipated to have on a headquarters element. In this specific target, there's also the additional issue of assets that could potentially be used for a reinforcing mission or some other movement to contact, and therefore fixing them, making them less likely to muster and move, is an additional element in this target.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, taking the Trial Chamber's direction, I'm not going to ask you about whether your opinion would change if there were no reinforcements in there. I'll take it, as I will for the remaining objectives, that if the factual situation changes your opinion potentially changes. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair enough. If there are no reinforcement, it influences that aspect of the analysis. It's still a headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to jump now to the open field outside of the northern barracks, which you address on page 33 at subsection (i). Here you offer the opinion that: "General Gotovina could have reasonably concluded that this field was one of only a few locations within Knin that enemy forces could use to muster prior to movement to contact or reinforcement. Accordingly, sporadically targeting this location would inhibit the ability of the enemy to do so and would contribute to denying the enemy's ability to manoeuvre at will." Now, Professor, you indicate this assumption about this field being one of only a few locations, but what I want to know is does your opinion include an assessment that it would be legitimate for General Gotovina to sporadically shell any area within Knin where the ARSK might possibly have mustered?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "might possibly" renders my answer no. But this was a field that I was told was in proximity to a barracks that I was told was a location where there were elements of a brigade, which in my mind is a unit that could be used -- be held in reserve by the corps -- the enemy corps commander. As a result, because of its proximity to the northern barracks, its nature as a place, in my view, is reasonably different than any open field in Knin. And again, if you -- this issue is also addressed in the commentary to Additional Protocol I, and that's why I say at the beginning in the abstract an open field would seem to hold little military value. But even Additional Protocol I addresses the use of methods and means of warfare to deny the enemy areas and acknowledges that in the right circumstances that is a logical, traditional, and appropriate use of combat capability. So the answer is yes -- or no to your question. I don't believe any open field in Knin falls into this same category, and that's because of the proximity to the forces that I was told to assume were in proximity to this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, in terms of what is reasonable for General Gotovina to anticipate or expect in relation to deciding to use artillery, in the middle of an artillery attack where anti-personnel and area weaponry is being used, do you really believe it's reasonable to expect that an army is going to choose to muster in an open field?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a coordinated operation to breach an improved enemy defensive perimeter that is protecting the enemy's political and military centre of gravity. If I am the attacking commander, I have to assume as part of my planning that if I achieve a breach, that breach will become the priority for the enemy's commitment of whatever reinforcing assets he can muster. So my answer to you is yes. I believe it would be reasonable to assume that even if under attack, if the corps commander, the enemy corps commander realises that his defensive positions have been breached, that he will do whatever he can do to plug that breach. Because once that breach is secured the other side begins to exploit it, and the decisive point of the battle has turned. And I have to assume my opponent knows that just as clearly as I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Corn, could I ask you, did you identify the other places which were fit to be used as -- to muster?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was asked to look at this field near this barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you said it was one of only a few locations, so you must have formed an opinion about how many there were and -- could you give the details about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That opinion was based on where I was told the manoeuvre forces within Knin were located. And in the facts and assumptions there is some Special Police units, and then I'm told there are elements of a brigade in this northern barracks. And so my assumption is that you're going to muster at -- you have to muster your forces from where they're housed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, let's move now to the RSK telegraph and post office, which you address on page 32, subsection (d). You state: "This classic 'dual use' target was an important component," of, "supporting" -- I'm sorry. " ... an important component supporting enemy communications ability. Degrading the effectiveness of such communications would provide a significant advantage to friendly forces seeking to set and maintain the tempo of battle." Professor, we've discussed this a bit already about the ability of General Gotovina to achieve a similar or the same effect by shelling in another area, but I'd like to, in regard to that, show you a portion of the Brioni meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could go to P461. And if we could turn to page 25 in the English, page 47 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I want to focus on where it begins Mladen Markac. "Mr. President, as soon as we take Celavac as a communications centre and to all practical purposes the nerve centre of that part, their communications system will be finished and there will be total chaos." Moving further down the page to where Davor Domazet speaks, the last paragraph where he speaks: "... and the destruction of Celavac, we will take down all operative and tactical communications in the area of the 7th and 15th Corps." Professor, you're aware that the 7th Corps area was the area of Knin; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if we could now have Exhibit P2625.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Here we have the report of the Croatian air force dated the 4th of August, indicating paragraph 2, number 1, the Celavac radio relay station was eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could now move to P2623. And if we could go to page 5 both in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And looking at the targets of the aircraft operation, subsection (b) it states: "During the first day neutralise the enemy units communication and command system, by using strikes against definite communication centre and command posts." Now, Professor, I know that you saw the Brioni transcript or at least reviewed it before coming to your conclusions. Did you consider the fact that the assessment made that by taking out Celavac, for all practical purposes, they would take out all operative and tactical communications?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated previously, I based this opinion on the facts and assumptions that counsel provided me after I requested that they make their assessment of what has been established on the record. The assumption, if not fact, related to the telegraph and post office was that 40 per cent of military communications were facilitated through this location. Now, the first report you showed me, I just briefly looked at the date time group, and I thought I noticed 2300 hours on 4 August. So if the air force reports the destruction of that relay facility, it certainly, if that's the time -- date/time group of that report, it certainly would not indicate to the -- to General Gotovina when he launches his attack, I believe on the morning of the 4th, that that capability is no longer existent. But even irrespective of that, I wrote this on the assumption that the -- that he believed, based on the record, that this facility provided 40 per cent of military communications capability. And if you're going to attack the UHF, VHF, and land-line capability at the headquarters, then you have to assume that the enemy is going to fall back on redundant communications capability. The other thing this report doesn't tell us is: Is the enemy capable of restoring that capability even if the air force has been successful? So there are -- in the abstract there are -- like everything else -- almost everything else we have discussed, there are other facts and circumstances that would be relevant in the decision-making process, but I base the assumption -- the opinion on the assumption that the commander assumed that this facility provided a military communications redundancy. If he knew that was not the case, it would have radically changed the equation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let's move now to the railway station, which you address on page 33, subsection (h). You state: "Harassing and disrupting movements through this critical rail choke-point would be an important means of limiting the effectiveness of enemy troop movements to reinforce isolated front line positions." Professor, I don't see where you were provided with any indication that the railway was being used to move enemy troops through Knin to the front line. Can you tell us whether or not that's a further assumption that you made?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's on page 4 of the letter, the second sentence of railway station says: "The rail system was to be used to evacuate a massive weapons depot and to reinforce the front lines."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies for that. Now, you indicate that it's a critical rail choke-point. Now, in line with what we discussed with the previous target, if you can, in fact, achieve the same objective by shelling parts of the railway line that will prevent both enemy front line reinforcement and evacuation of a weapons depot, if you can shell the rail lines in areas not proximate to civilians, aren't you required to do that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the resource expenditure is analogous, then the answer is yes. But I think that that is a reason why traditionally when you target lines of communication, you look for choke-points because you can use a limited amount of resources to affect a major amount of movement. That's what "choke-point" means to me, a crossroads or an intersection. But if there's only one line and you know that's the only line the enemy's going to use and you can destroy it outside of the town with no additional significant additional expenditure of resources or risk, I am confident that the protocol requires you to adopt that alternate course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, I want you to assume that this has been a real pleasure for me. I appreciate your sticking with me, and I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Kehoe, could you give us an indication as to how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will be very brief. I would just like to chat with my client just for a bit before we go on, but I will not be extensive at all. Anywhere from 2 minutes to maybe 15 minutes, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the best would be to take the break now and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the other Defence teams are concerned, has the cross-examination triggered any need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- examine the witness? I see, Mr. Cayley, you're nodding "no" as well. Then we'll first have a break. We will resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Cross-examination has not brought up any issues that need to be addressed in re-direct, so we will have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Corn, Professor Corn, you know what the consequences of this will be, that what you consider to be a break was already the end of your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming even twice to The Hague in order to give your testimony, both in the beginning of the week and then later this week, and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and the Bench. And I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would like to thank the Tribunal first for supporting my effort to keep the commitment that I had made previously in the middle of the week; and secondly, for indulging some long answers at times. I do appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Usher, could you escort Professor Corn out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there any remaining matters of documents to be tendered or are we concluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The only issue I think is D1462, the report is MFI'd and we would once again re-offer that into evidence. Is it 1462? Excuse me 1462, I believe it is. I stand corrected, it is 1462.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 1642. Dyslexia is overwhelming here, 1642.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we made objections to the admission of certain sections of the report. Those objections still stand. On top of that, we would like to make further submissions. I don't know if the Court wants to hear those orally or if you prefer a written submission. I'm happy to do it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to hear them right now, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In addition to the arguments put forward in our submission in response to the 94 bis filing, I think the testimony of the witness has raised to an even greater level the concerns of transparency and of notice to the Prosecution. As the Court itself recognised, it is a bit of a grey area for us to know exactly what the witness's evidence is based on. This oral presentation he was provided with in December of 2008, we still don't know what he was told. He seems to recall portions of it at times. When I confronted him with some pieces of evidence that didn't seem to be supported by the facts and assumptions, he went back to rely on that conversation. I think that just highlights the fact that neither the Trial Chamber nor the Prosecution is aware of what his report actually is based on. It also seriously impacted the Prosecution's ability to confront him and to challenge the basis for his evidence. It also led to us not being able to truly discover his analysis since we don't know what that analysis was based on. So I think in addition to the arguments we made before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- take a breath now and then, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I do think the lack of transparency with regard to the sources of information and the information upon which the opinions are based justify the Chamber in refusing to accept the portions we've identified as well as the lack of notice to the Prosecution with respect to the opinions he had on the critical documents. The Chamber had to await the Prosecution's examination in order to find out what the witness thought of the order for attack language, what the witness thought about the Brioni transcript. And I'll highlight again, Your Honour, that if we had not received the supplemental information sheet, it would have been a simple matter for us to simply point out the evidence that he had not considered; but having the one-liner that we got in the supplemental information sheet which simply says: I considered all this evidence and it doesn't change my opinion, it incorporated all of the substance of that critical evidence into his analysis which we were forced to confront without notice. So I think on that basis we would ask the Chamber not to admit the portions we identified in our notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, perhaps you first take a breath for Mr. Russo, and then make further submissions. If you would like to make them orally or if you would prefer to do it in a different way, we would hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will make it very brief, Mr. President. With regard to the issue of transparency in this regard, that was the reason why we went through this extensive cross-examination, to elicit the basis -- bases upon which Professor Corn rendered his opinions. He told the Chamber that he had had a briefing concerning the overall scheme of things in December of 2008. I do believe on certainly more than one occasion -- in fact, numerous occasions, Professor Corn stated that he gave his opinions based on the facts and assumptions provided in the report which were attached to his report. Nothing more, nothing less. If anything, the transparency was ultimately borne out by the fact that Professor Corn said, Mr. Russo, if you change the facts and circumstances, the opinions I have rendered could change. To what extent of course depends on that. Now, the argument that was presented by counsel that there was some lack of transparency because there was no opinion or notice of an opinion concerning what he thought about P1125, the attack order from the 3rd of August, or what he thought about the Brioni transcript, I remind counsel -- and I have to say to the Chamber that we did not elicit those opinions on direct examination. If we go back to the direct examination, our direct examination was very terse, very succinct, and was rendered and presented to the Chamber in support of D1462, Professor Corn's report -- 1642, I did it again, Professor Corn's report. That was the basis of our direct examination, simply to offer any clarifications of D1642, the report. So the statements made by counsel have no bearing on the admission of this report. Now he, Mr. Russo, chose of his own volition to go into the matters concerning the attack order and matters concerning Brioni and any number of other items. Now, we gave notice to the Office of the Prosecutor that this individual did, in fact, review these documents. If there was some problem with that, I submit to the Chamber that we should have heard about that prior to cross-examination. But nevertheless, if we go back to how this all proceeded, it proceeded by us putting -- the Gotovina Defence putting this witness on to offer D16 -- his -- 1642, his report, into evidence. Anything else that emanated from that concerning this cross-examination was brought about by the Office of the Prosecutor, not by the Gotovina Defence. If we go back to the rule, the question is: Have we established enough basis under the rule to allow the Chamber to consider this report and give it the weight in conjunction with Professor Corn's testimony that it deserves. And I would submit to you, Mr. President, and the Chamber that we -- the Gotovina Defence has more than established a bases upon which this report should be received into evidence in conjunction with Professor Corn's report. I would gladly clarify any aspects of this submission, this oral submission, that we've made, or do so in writing should the Chamber so need additional arguments presented to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you emphasised that the -- going through the Brioni transcript was an exercise by the Prosecution. Now, I would like to know your view on the following. The Brioni transcript raises a couple of issues of interpretation, that is, what President Tudjman said, how the response had to be understood in relation to what was said, et cetera, et cetera. And I gained some impression - I still have to digest that and to read everything in detail - that the -- this interpretation of what the witness apparently read in the Brioni transcript may have been of influence on his further developing his opinion on events. We do not find the precise conclusions of the expert witness on the Brioni transcript, the issues I just referred to. Nevertheless, as I said, I gained the impression that -- I wouldn't say decisive, but at least they played a role in further assessing situations. My question to you now is that saying to Mr. Russo, Well, that's the matter you raised, do you think that in terms of transparency of the methods, of the whole line of thought of the expert, that it would have been preferable or not preferable to have this already explained before cross-examination? Because you're more or less saying, Well, that's your problem, Mr. Russo, you raised it. So you considered it -- if Mr. Russo would not have raised it, you would have considered it that the Chamber would have been sufficiently informed about the way in which the expert developed his opinions without knowing how he interpreted - and I'm now just referring to this one document - that he had, as he said, considered in forming his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There are several issues, if I may take them seriatim, Mr. President, first with regard to the Brioni transcript or all of the documents that are listed in the supplemental information sheet, none of those documents were provided to Professor Corn until after he filed the first part of his report and the addendum. None of those documents were discussed. So the opinion that we were placing or the position we were placing before the Trial Chamber was concretised prior to any discussion about these documents. Now, we had a discussion about these documents in discussing this matter with Professor Corn so the professor would have an idea of what was happening in cross-examination. Now, you recall, Mr. President, there was a motion filed by the Office of the Prosecutor barring us from using, for instance, P1125. And I came in -- I certainly told the Court Officer, and I believe we put it on the record, that we were not going to go into those documents, nor were we going into the Brioni transcript. So what we presented to the Trial Chamber was -- and to the Office of the Prosecutor was full transparency to support what Professor Corn was opining upon with his report and his addendum. We were not going to elicit any discussion concerning the attack order or Brioni or any other number of documents, but counsel chose to do so. So -- while I Your Honour sifting your way through this, and I'm sure as the trier of fact, Your Honours, Mr. President, it's a difficult matter to wind your way through. But putting that all aside, it doesn't affect the basic argument or the basic document D1642, Professor Corn's report, that we were presenting the Chamber. Had counsel not asked these questions about Brioni or about the attack order, P1125, we would not have had this protracted discussion. But counsel chose to do so. At the same time counsel told -- wanted to preclude us from going into it on direct, and we took the high ground, frankly, Mr. President, and didn't go into it on direct because we didn't want to get into some debate as to whether or not that -- that Professor Corn was offering some opinion about these documents that were -- that was not included in his report because, frankly, he hadn't seen them until after his report was filed. So it is -- the position taken by the Prosecutor is double-edged in the sense that we're not supposed to show him these reports, we don't want you to show him these reports, but we want to. That's simply not how this works, that's not how the exercise works. The Prosecution has put a year's-plus witnesses on where they'd clearly in discussing these matters with their witnesses, presented it to those witnesses that this is what the Gotovina Defence or other Defences are going to bring up on cross-examination. That, in the spirit of transparency, is what counsel should do and did do. We simply did the same thing. Again I have to reiterate, in our direct examination -- our direct examination was centred in focused solely on the four corners of Professor Corn's report; nothing more, nothing less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Mr. Kehoe, at the start of the testimony of this witness we had the report which was produced without the witness having had read the Brioni transcript and other documents, but we also had the one line Mr. Russo referred to, that having looked at these documents that it would not affect the conclusions, which as was shown during cross-examination was to some extent viewed to the way in which he interpreted that. So you're very much emphasising that the report was produced without. But would you agree that the Chamber was not only -- of course you could say admission of the report is just a report. But what is true for an expert report is, of course, true for expert testimony as well, that is, that the Chamber is able to have a full insight in the reasoning, the thinking, the forming of the opinion, the method used, and that the Chamber under those circumstances - and you're blaming Mr. Russo more or less for doing that - might have been interested in knowing what interpretations of these documents were at the basis of they do not change my opinion. Because that took quite some thinking from what I understood from the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I submit to you and suggest to you -- I will say at the outset, I'm not blaming counsel for anything. Counsel prepared his witnesses in a similar fashion, no doubt because I was on that side of the well for many years, that they prepare their witnesses for cross-examination as good counsel have done. They did the same thing. The supplemental information sheet, fundamentally, was emanated from the issue of transparency. Your Honour has asked questions of General Cross and others concerning transparency. We thought it was incumbent on us to ensure that there was no stone unturned when it came to transparency. We were not going to say that this witness didn't examine documents when he was sitting at our office preparing for this examination which started on Monday. To that end, we delineated every document that he was shown. Now, with regard to the other aspects as to where his opinion started and his opinion began concerning his statement -- his statement and how it might have been affected, we were here for four days of cross-examination on that score. That is the purpose of cross-examination. We could have gone through that and elicited that in some detail as to whether or not this affected your opinion; and if not, why not? And we did do that to some degree with P1125. We didn't do it with the rest of them because counsel chose not to and chose a different methodology in his cross, as is his professional discretion. But the fact remains that what we have attempted to do from the very outset, Mr. President, Your Honours, is transparency, is going through the procedure, is going through exactly what took place, when and where this person was spoken to by counsel for General Gotovina, what he was shown and when, and any conclusions or aspects that he might have had as a result of that subsequent review, that the Chamber needed to be advised of as well as the Office of the Prosecutor. So -- I mean, the cross-examination is something that could have done this. Counsel chose not to. And I submit to Your Honour, if there is some question in that regard, I suspect that Professor Corn is still here in town, and we can continue this this afternoon and bring him back and we can ask him yet more questions about this. The Gotovina Defence is interested in the ultimate in transparency, and if that needs to be done, Mr. President, we invite the Chamber to do that, to clarify any outstanding issues in this regard because this is very, very significant. And this is something that we were mindful of when we were preparing this witness and preparing the supplemental information sheet. Counsel chose not to ask these questions on cross; that's his decision, but, however, that doesn't lend itself to a conclusion that there has been some lack of transparency concerning this witness's conclusions and answers before this Trial Chamber over the past four days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President. I don't agree with the distinction that Mr. Kehoe is drawing between the questions he asked Professor Corn during his examination and the evidence in fact led by the Defence during their direct examination. The supplemental information sheet is Exhibit D1643. When they admitted that into evidence, they essentially led the opinion that he considered the Brioni transcript and all of the other documents and that it didn't change his opinion. The fact that they didn't specifically ask him those questions again doesn't make any difference. So the objection that we had originally made to him being shown the documents and him offering an opinion about that, we were essentially pre-empted on that argument by them having already shown it to him and having already solicited an opinion from him with respect to that. That opinion was led through direct examination, and at that point we were compelled to cross-examine on it. I will be very clear. If that opinion had not been led, the Prosecution would not have gone into the order for attack or the Brioni transcript or any of the other documents about which we received a late opinion about his conclusion. And with respect to the last comments that counsel made, it's unclear to me what he's saying that we chose not to do in terms of going into the basis for his report. I did ask the witness to tell me everything he could recall about the information he received at the oral presentation. Of course with no fault to him, he simply can't give us a full account of that information, and that's the position that the Prosecution finds itself in as well as the Trial Chamber, and that is a result of the method which the Defence chose to employ. They could simply have provided us with either, I don't know, a transcript or some other recording of the actual discussion they had with them so that we would know in fact what he was provided with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may respond, with all due respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the Defence is the party tendering the report. Mr. Russo objected. He has been the last that spoke, being the responding party. You both have 1 minute. You first, and then Mr. Russo, and then we'll conclude this -- these submissions. If you make it two, I'm not going to blame you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will not. I will make it one, maybe 1 minute and 15 seconds. First thing of course is at the outset, if we look at the proofing session of the 21st of September, 2008, which was Colonel Konings' proofing session where we asked the Prosecution to disclose the substance of that proofing session, Mr. Russo, himself, declined, but that's another issue. With regard to the supplemental information sheet which is D1643, the subject was raised by that -- by the Chamber. Mr. Russo objected to the last portion of paragraph 2 and paragraph 3. He did not object to anything else in that; and given that, we have deleted that, uploaded into e-court, admitted into evidence, and he had no objection to the rest of the document. We can go back and verify in the record exactly what Mr. Russo said. I don't have it before me, but I'm firmly convinced that that was the position. That being the case, the point that -- at that -- at this juncture or that juncture was to object to the whole matter, but he chose not to do so. Now we are in a revisionist-history mode, where he's trying to change that. He didn't object. We took out that which he objected to in conjunction with consultation with the Chambers, and we admitted D64, and he didn't object to the portion of the supplemental information sheet that Professor Corn opined that the review of these documents wouldn't change his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My judgement that you would need 2 minutes was rather exact, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Russo, 2 minutes for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, all I can say in response to that is we had already made our submissions on our objections to the admissibility of opinions relating to those three particular documents. I don't think procedurally we were required to re-state that particular objection. Our submissions on that were before the Trial Chamber. In the Defence's submission of that document, I took it to be the Trial Chamber's ruling that our objections had been overruled. In any case we had made our objections to the Trial Chamber about the admission of that evidence. At that point, I don't believe we were required to reiterate those objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. The Chamber will consider the matter, and the Chamber will rule on the matter. We will not sit this afternoon. We'll not sit on Monday. Is there any matter that should be raised before Tuesday, when we'll hear the Gotovina Defence's next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if we wish to admit the 92 bis statements. I believe there are seven remaining, if you wish to do that now or at a different time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you wish to admit -- that's what the transcript tells me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We wish to admit, but if you wish to do that now, or if we're going to do it at some other point in time. These are the 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, out of which four we have -- four witnesses became 92 ter witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- several witnesses still being 92 bis. Do you want to make further submissions, or do you want us to admit them right away, or to deny admission or?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't wish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's for the Chamber to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, I understood the Prosecution's position - maybe I'm wrong - that they just wanted to cross-examine four, and then they had no objection to the admission of the remaining 92 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That -- yes, but even under those circumstances, still the Chamber has to decide whatever the -- but the position of the Prosecution was that there was no objection against admission if you could cross-examine four of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll admit, I'm a bit ignorant of the exact language of our filing, but we certainly haven't changed the position that we filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the Chamber can proceed and consider the matter on the basis of the written submissions by the Prosecution. Then we'll rule on admission, and we'll do that rather soon. Any other matter? Then we'll adjourn, and we'll resume on Tuesday, the 15th of September, 9.00, in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of September, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.21 p.m.,
